researchers.name: Paul A. Kirschner
researchers.known_for: Lead author of 'Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work' (2006, with Sweller and Clark) — argues novices need explicit direct instruction and that minimally guided/discovery approaches cause cognitive overload

researchers.name: John Sweller
researchers.known_for: Cognitive Load Theory; co-author of the 2006 minimal-guidance critique; worked-example effect showing studying solutions beats unguided problem-solving for novices

researchers.name: Manu Kapur
researchers.known_for: Productive Failure — carefully designed problem-solving BEFORE instruction improves conceptual learning, but only when followed by teacher-led consolidation; distinguishes productive failure from unguided discovery

researchers.name: Kurt VanLehn
researchers.known_for: 2011 meta-analysis: human tutoring effect size 0.79 vs no tutoring; step-based computer tutoring nearly as effective (0.76); challenged the '2-sigma' folklore about tutoring

researchers.name: Arnav Gudibande and Eric Wallace
researchers.affiliation: UC Berkeley (with Snell, Geng, Liu, Abbeel, Levine, Song)
researchers.known_for: 'The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs' (2023) — small models fine-tuned on teacher outputs imitate style, not capability; crowdworker ratings are misleading

researchers.name: Mrinmaya Sachan (with David Dinucu-Jianu, Jakub Macina, Nico Daheim, Ido Hakimi, Iryna Gurevych)
researchers.affiliation: ETH Zurich / ETH AI Center / TU Darmstadt
researchers.known_for: 'From Problem-Solving to Teaching Problem-Solving' — online RL alignment turning a 7B model into a tutor that withholds solutions (10.6% leakage) while improving simulated student solve rates 25.3%, near-matching proprietary LearnLM

researchers.name: Andrew Lan
researchers.known_for: Training LLM-based tutors to optimize actual student learning outcomes in dialogues (AIED 2025), rather than optimizing for surface helpfulness

researchers.name: Hoda Fakour and Moslem Imani
researchers.affiliation: National Taiwan Normal University / National Taiwan University
researchers.known_for: 2025 mixed-methods study (N=230) comparing ChatGPT vs human tutors on critical thinking: humans rated higher for critical-thinking encouragement (4.5 vs 4.2) and personalized feedback (4.6 vs 3.8); AI rated far higher for comfort in asking questions (4.9 vs 2.8)

frameworks.name: Cognitive Load Theory
frameworks.description: Working-memory limits mean novices learn less from unguided problem search; explicit guidance and worked examples reduce extraneous load. Basis of the Kirschner/Sweller/Clark case against minimal guidance; guidance can fade as expertise grows (expertise reversal)

frameworks.name: Productive Failure
frameworks.description: Kapur's sequencing framework: structured struggle on a well-designed problem BEFORE explicit instruction, followed by mandatory teacher-led consolidation connecting learner attempts to formal concepts. Explicitly NOT unguided discovery

frameworks.name: Pedagogical RL alignment (student-simulation reward)
frameworks.description: ETH framework: tutor LLM trained via online RL against a simulated student, rewarded jointly for student solve-rate gains and low solution leakage (a lambda tradeoff parameter balances pedagogy vs helpfulness), preserving base capabilities better than SFT-based Socratic tuning

frameworks.name: Superficial Alignment Hypothesis (LIMA)
frameworks.description: Zhou et al. 2023: almost all model knowledge is learned in pretraining; alignment/fine-tuning mainly teaches style and format — 1,000 curated examples sufficed for LIMA. Explains both why small-data behavior tuning works for format and why it fails to add capability

frameworks.name: Behavior-aware sampling for safe fine-tuning
frameworks.description: Selecting safety/constraint examples by instruction-response behavior (refusal vs compliance) plus semantic diversity across harm categories to prevent catastrophic forgetting; up to 41% harmfulness reduction with only 0.05% added training data

frameworks.name: Pedagogical ability evaluation taxonomy for AI tutors
frameworks.description: Unified taxonomy (Maurya et al.) for judging LLM tutor responses on dimensions like mistake identification, providing guidance, and NOT revealing the answer too early — used to benchmark tutor models beyond generic helpfulness

debates.positions: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006): minimally guided instruction is significantly less effective and less efficient for novices; decades of evidence favor direct guidance. Kapur: struggle before instruction improves conceptual understanding — but both camps agree explicit instruction and structure are required; the real disagreement is sequencing, not whether to guide

debates.topic: Can small models be turned into real tutors by imitating big-model behavior?
debates.positions: Optimists (Alpaca/Vicuna era): fine-tuning on teacher outputs makes small models competitive. Gudibande et al.: imitation transfers style/fluency, not capability — the gap persists except on tasks heavily covered in imitation data. Middle position (ETH RL tutor, LIMA): narrow BEHAVIORAL constraints (question-asking, answer-withholding, format) are exactly the thing small-data tuning CAN instill, even though broad capability cannot be

debates.topic: Is rated 'helpfulness' a valid signal of tutoring quality?
debates.positions: Preference-trained LLMs and their judges reward giving direct answers; pedagogy researchers argue helpfulness-as-judged anticorrelates with sound tutoring (withholding answers, prompting reasoning). A pre-registered audit found LLM-judged helpfulness is an unreliable pedagogy signal across tutor models

Fakour & Imani: humans still superior for critical-thinking encouragement, personalized feedback, emotional intelligence, and trust; AI superior for self-paced learning and judgment-free question-asking (4.9 vs 2.8) — suggesting complementary roles rather than replacement

findings.claim: Human tutoring raises test scores ~0.79 SD vs no tutoring; step-based intelligent tutoring is nearly as effective (0.76), undercutting the assumption that human Socratic dialogue is uniquely powerful
Median effect of intelligent tutoring systems across 50 evaluations: +0.66 SD (50th to 75th percentile)
findings.source: Kulik & Fletcher, Review of Educational Research

findings.claim: Imitation models (1.5B-13B, 0.3M-150M imitation tokens) close little to none of the base-model-to-ChatGPT gap on tasks not covered in imitation data, despite crowdworkers rating outputs competitive with ChatGPT; they mimic style but not factuality
findings.source: Gudibande et al., 'The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs'

findings.claim: A 7B model RL-aligned for pedagogy reached 25.3% simulated-student solve-rate improvement with only 10.6% solution leakage, nearly matching LearnLM's leakage, while base benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MATH500) moved only -0.6% to +1.4%; the SFT baseline SocraticLM lost -2.1% MMLU and -9.4% MATH500
findings.source: Dinucu-Jianu et al., 'From Problem-Solving to Teaching Problem-Solving'

findings.claim: Fine-tuning on benign data catastrophically erodes prior safety/refusal behavior; changes in instruction adherence are the main driver of the degradation
findings.source: Interpretable Catastrophic Forgetting via Instruction Vector; Behavior-Aware Sampling

findings.claim: Mixing a tiny, behaviorally targeted set of constraint examples (0.05% additional data selected by refusal-vs-compliance behavior and harm-category diversity) into fine-tuning cuts harmfulness up to 41% — targeted data selection preserves constraints cheaply
Catastrophic forgetting during instruction tuning generally worsens with model scale within 1B-7B ranges, making constraint retention a first-order concern for small-model fine-tunes
findings.source: Revisiting Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Model Tuning

findings.claim: Students rated human tutors higher than ChatGPT for critical-thinking encouragement (4.5 vs 4.2), personalized feedback (4.6 vs 3.8), and complex-concept understanding (4.8 vs 4.0); ChatGPT won on self-paced learning (4.8 vs 3.9) and comfort asking questions (4.9 vs 2.8)
findings.source: Fakour & Imani, Frontiers in Education (N=230 Taiwanese university students)

findings.claim: Khanmigo operationalizes answer-withholding via prompt design and educator-feedback iteration ('productive struggle'); evaluating whether a tutor avoids revealing answers too early still requires expert human rating of multi-turn dialogues
findings.source: Unifying AI Tutor Evaluation taxonomy; LLM-Tutor overview

findings.claim: Problem-solving before instruction (productive failure) improved conceptual understanding of variance without harming procedural fluency — but only with canonical consolidation afterward

misconceptions.belief: A good Socratic tutor never gives answers — withholding is always pedagogically superior
misconceptions.reality: Unstructured Socratic questioning risks digression and superficial engagement; both the direct-instruction camp and productive-failure camp require explicit instruction/consolidation. Withholding helps only within a structured sequence with adequate guidance, and novices under high cognitive load can be actively harmed by pure discovery

misconceptions.belief: Human preference ratings (crowdworkers or LLM judges) are a good proxy for tutor/model quality
misconceptions.reality: Crowdworkers rated imitation models competitive with ChatGPT while targeted evals showed almost no capability gain; LLM-judged 'helpfulness' is an unreliable pedagogy signal because helpfulness training rewards giving answers away

misconceptions.belief: Fine-tuning a small model on a large teacher's outputs transfers the teacher's competence
misconceptions.reality: It transfers surface style and format, not knowledge or reasoning; capability gaps persist except on tasks heavily represented in the imitation data. However, narrow behavioral policies (tone, format, answer-withholding) are precisely what small-data tuning CAN reliably instill (LIMA's superficial alignment hypothesis)

misconceptions.belief: Fine-tuning on benign, on-task data leaves a model's prior constraints and safety behavior intact
misconceptions.reality: Catastrophic forgetting degrades refusal/constraint adherence even from benign fine-tuning; retention requires deliberate mitigation such as behavior-aware mixing of constraint exemplars (as little as 0.05% extra data can recover much of it)

misconceptions.belief: Direct instruction and productive struggle are irreconcilable opposites
misconceptions.reality: Productive failure embeds explicit instruction after structured struggle; Kirschner/Sweller/Clark allow guidance fading with expertise. The empirical disagreement is about sequencing and learner prior knowledge, not about whether guidance is needed
